hint.spinta: The doctor steps off at the Pier at eight. At one he must open the Pharmacy.
hint.indizio: Lunardi cures whoever is beneath him. Gino in bed won't move: the doctor must reach him.

arrivo.1: Dr Ettore Lunardi, pharmacist, from Padua. Delighted, truly delighted.
arrivo.2: Nobody shakes his hand. The ferry pulls away and he stays there, with two suitcases.

cura.1: He put a hand on his forehead, the way you do with children, and the fever went down.
cura.2: I still don't know whether to thank him or send him back to Padua on the first ferry.

noncura.1: Gino is still burning. The stranger walked right past him without stopping.
noncura.2: To cure someone I must pass over them, madam. Like a blanket. Do forgive me.

nina.1: Thirty-eight and a half. I'll read chapter thirty-one in bed, with the proper fever.
nina.2: I caught it from whoever caught it from Gino. It goes from hand to hand, like books.

teresa.1: He passed me and said “excuse me”. Who says excuse me, here? Nobody, dear.
teresa.2: And he touched my bag. The whole island's post, brushed by a stranger.

marta.testo: Gino has been burning for three days, and for the first time in his life he lies still in bed. That mainland doctor is to see him by noon, and by tomorrow evening he's to be well. I'll bring the man his bread.

esito.ok: The doctor saw to Gino before noon. Cured, Gino started running again: Marta says she preferred the fever.
esito.fallita: Gino is still burning. Marta put the doctor's bread at the bottom of the basket, under yesterday's.

teresa.testo: Dear, a doctor arrives from Padua tomorrow morning, one who knows nobody. Keep him away from me: I've the whole island's post in my bag, and some things are not to be touched.
teresa.r1: Teresa, the doctor is here to cure people, not to read the post.
teresa.r2: All right. He'll keep to the other end of the Fondamenta, I promise.

esito.ok: The doctor and Teresa never crossed. The island's post stayed untouched, and so did Teresa, she says.
esito.fallita: The stranger crossed Teresa on the Fondamenta. She counted the envelopes twice, then three times.

nina.testo: In The Betrothed the plague takes nearly everyone. I've no time for chapter thirty-one: don't let the fever reach me. Don't tell Dad, or he won't sleep.

esito.ok: The fever never found Nina. She read until late, to celebrate.
esito.fallita: The fever reached Nina too, hand to hand. Nobody has told her dad, for now.

margine.febbre: Fever asks no leave: whoever crosses a sick thread, from above or below, falls ill.
margine.ginoLetto: Gino with a fever stays in bed: while he is ill he doesn't have to run.
margine.cura: Lunardi above a sick thread cures it. But Gino, once cured, starts running again.

hint.spinta: Two sick: Gino gives the fever to whoever he crosses. Bakery and church stay open.
hint.indizio: Lunardi never falls ill: put him between the sick and the well, and keep him on top.

quarantena.1: On the Fondamenta people walk single file, an arm's length apart. The bakery stays open.
quarantena.2: The Lord counts those who pray at home too. I count the ones who cough.

marta.1: I held Gino in my arms all afternoon. He's burning, but he laughs, the little wretch.
marta.2: If I fall ill too, the Lord can knead the bread. His hands are clean.

bepi.1: The stranger put a hand on my head, and the fever went. Just like that.
bepi.2: Don't go telling people. Nina least of all.

chiuso.1: Mr Scarpa shut the door in my face. Twice, the second time harder.
chiuso.2: A fever left alone doesn't pass: it walks. Tomorrow it will have another name.

piero.1: I said mass with a fever. I blessed the healthy and coughed over the pews.
piero.2: The Lord forgives. Fever doesn't. Tomorrow I'll say mass from the window.

marta.testo: They say keep the well away from the sick. I stay with my Gino, fever or no fever: after noon I want him near me. I'll shut the bakery for an hour, and the hungry can wait.
marta.r1: Stay with him, Marta. The bakery can wait an hour. Gino can't.
marta.r2: Gino won't go away like Ernesto, Marta. I promise you.

senzaArchivio.r2: Gino will get better, Marta. And he'll stay here, with you.

esito.ok: Marta kept Gino close all afternoon. If she caught the fever, she won't tell anyone.
esito.fallita: Gino spent the afternoon away from Marta. She kneaded until evening, without looking up.

lunardi.testo: Dear Miss Lacemaker, I beg you: at least three visits tomorrow, and call on the fisherman Scarpa too, who won't open his door to me. One does not argue with fever. With fishermen, one does.

esito.ok: The doctor made his visits, and the fisherman Scarpa opened his door to him. Once.
esito.fallita: The doctor knocked and knocked again. His rounds stayed half done, and the fever went about on its own.

piero.testo: Tomorrow I'll say eleven o'clock mass for the healthy, and the sick will pray at home. But the priest at least must stay well: or who will say it? Help me, my child. Deo gratias.

esito.ok: The fever never got into the church. At eleven the pews were half empty, but the priest was on his feet.
esito.fallita: The priest fell ill. At eleven the healthy prayed on their own, and the Lord listened all the same.

bepi.testo: that doctor from away dont come in my house. the fevver I keep, it pases by itself like bad weather. and dont tel nina nothing
bepi.r1: Bepi, let him see you. Do it for Nina, if not for yourself.
bepi.r2: All right. The doctor stays outside, and you keep your fever.

esito.ok: The doctor never crossed Bepi. Nina nursed his fever, with broth and a sharp tongue.
esito.fallita: The doctor got to Bepi. The door opened a hand's breadth, and then a little more.

hint.spinta: If Teresa and Marta cross, they knot: nothing passes and they stand still an hour.
hint.indizio: The report must go round the knot: from Teresa to whoever's below her, and on to Marta.

nodo.1: On the bakery doorstep the two threads knotted. Neither woman spoke.
nodo.2: Thirty years, and my stomach still knots. Like the first day.

giro.1: I went round the back, behind the nets. As always, for thirty years.
giro.2: A knot not tied is a knot that stays. Grandmother used to say so.

pagella.1: WELL DONE! It says WELL DONE! With a big W and a line under it!
pagella.2: Cake tonight. But the report, who brought it? Not Teresa, I hope.

letta.1: Teresa's still got my report. She read all of it, even the back!
letta.2: Well done in Italian, dear. In arithmetic, less so. But your mum won't hear it from me.

porta.1: She saw me coming and went back in. She shut the bakery door, quietly.
porta.2: Thirty years, dear. And I know exactly why, which is the worst of it.

teresa.testo: Dear, it's been thirty years. Tomorrow morning I want to speak to Marta, even just on the bakery doorstep, even just for a minute. Let me meet her. I'll say the rest.

esito.ok: Teresa and Marta came face to face, after thirty years. They said nothing, but neither lowered her eyes.
esito.fallita: Teresa and Marta did not meet. Teresa said “never mind, dear” in the voice of someone counting years.

marta.testo: I don't want to see Teresa. Not tomorrow, not ever. Thirty years I've steered clear of her, and tomorrow I will too. I know the way with my eyes shut.
marta.r1: What did she do to you, Marta, thirty years ago? Tell me, and maybe I'll understand.
marta.r2: All right. Steer clear of her, if it makes you feel better.

esito.ok: Marta didn't cross Teresa, not even from behind. Tonight her bread came out hard.
esito.fallita: Marta found Teresa in front of her, on the doorstep. She gripped her apron until her knuckles went white.

gino.testo: the teecher gave me my report and it sez WELL DONE!!! teresa has got it. get it to mum before 2 so tomorow nite she makes me the cake. the one with apples

esito.ok: The report reached Marta before two. Tonight there's apple cake, and Gino has already eaten half.
esito.fallita: The report stayed in Teresa's bag. Gino waited for the cake until evening, and nothing.

margine.nodo: Two who hate each other, if they meet, stand still: an hour knotted, giving nothing.

margine.nome: Who names you, keeps you. Before weaving, I pin my name on a thread.

hint.spinta: Bepi leaves on the nine o'clock ferry that brings the doctor back. You pin the name.
hint.indizio: The name passes like a rumour. Whoever knows of the debt mustn't cross Nina.

nome.1: Last night I pinned my name on a thread, like a button on a jacket.
nome.2: In the mirror, my figurine has lost a little colour. Only a little.

lunardi.1: Ada. Ada Vio. A fine name, short and precise, like a good prescription.
lunardi.1d: They told me your name, miss. And already it escapes me, forgive me.
lunardi.2: I'll write it in my prescription book, so as not to lose it. There: in capitals.

lunardi_no.1: I asked everyone. “The little one”, “the lacemaker”. Nobody can say more.
lunardi_no.2: Strange place: here a name must be passed from hand to hand, like bread.

debito.1: Dad owes money to half of Chioggia. I heard it at the Pier, from the street.
debito.2: He's gone to pay them. With what, I wonder. With the boat, maybe.

faro.1: From three on I watched the sea towards Chioggia. Nothing. Only gulls.
faro.2: You don't forget handwriting, little one. Not even after fourteen years.
faro.2d: You don't forget handwriting, miss. Not even after fourteen years.

lunardi.testo: Forgive the question, I have wondered for a week: what is the lacemaker's name? Tomorrow I come back on the nine o'clock ferry, and I shall ask at least three people. One will know.

esito.ok: The doctor learned my name. He greeted me by it three times, like someone trying out a new word.
esito.fallita: The doctor never learned my name. He greeted me with a bow, “miss”, the way one greets a stranger.

bepi.testo: tomoro morning I go to chiogia on the 9 ferry to setle a thing. nina mustnt know about the debt. nothing. I wil see to it
bepi.r1: Sooner or later she'll know, Bepi. Better from you than from the street.
bepi.r2: She won't hear it from me, Bepi. But the island is small, and Teresa's tongue is long.

esito.ok: Nina heard nothing about the debt. Bepi came back from Chioggia with empty pockets and the face of a man who has settled everything.
esito.fallita: Nina heard about the debt from the street, before she heard it from her dad. Tonight nobody talks in the Scarpa house.

zeno.testo: Tomorrow I'm coming down for eleven o'clock mass, to talk to the priest. From three the Lighthouse is mine: no visitors. I have a handwriting to ponder.

esito.ok: Zeno stayed alone on the Lighthouse after three. When he came down he had the eyes of a man who has reread an old letter.
esito.fallita: Zeno didn't have the Lighthouse to himself. He grumbled at the wind until evening.

teresa.testo: Dear, Bepi owes money to half of Chioggia, everyone knows but his daughter. It isn't right, at seventeen you're grown. Let Nina know it before two.

esito.ok: Teresa wanted Nina to know, and Nina knows. Teresa has the air of someone who has done a good deed.
esito.fallita: Nina found out nothing before two. Teresa said “just as well” with the face of someone who doesn't mean it.

perline.febbre: the fever of the four sick

hint.spinta: Four sick and only one doctor. Tonight's thread is enough for two visits, not for all.
hint.indizio: Whoever is cured and then crosses a sick one falls ill again: the last visits count.

specchio.1: A whole day of visits. I have never walked so much, not even in Padua.
specchio.2: In the chest, a lace from 1958 has the same shape as last night's.

gino.1: He ate two whole loaves. He's well, the little wretch. I thank whoever I must.
gino.2: Mum, Granny always said keep still. Not me! I run!

nina.1: Thirty-six point eight. The doctor says I'm his best patient. I'm his only one.
nina.2: He also says Leopardi is bad for your health. He's wrong, but he's sweet.

piero.1: The boy got me cured. On Sunday he rings the bell, he insisted.
piero.2: Out of tune, of course. Like everything on this island. Like me.

bepi.1: The fever still has me. Nina isn't studying, she's looking after me.
bepi.2: The doctor never got as far as me. He says last night there wasn't thread for all.

marta.testo: Gino is raving and calling for Granny. Yours. Says she told him to keep still. Let the doctor see him by five, and him be well by evening. I'm asking you please.

esito.ok: The doctor saw Gino in time, and by evening he was cured: he started running at once. Marta let him, for once.
esito.fallita: Gino still has the fever, and calls for Grandmother in his sleep. Marta sits up by his bed.

lunardi.testo: Miss Lacemaker, I have medicine for all but legs for one. The Scarpa girl has fever and books on her bed: I must see her by four, and she must mend. I rely on you. On you, miss, I mean.
lunardi.r1: Thank you, Doctor. We'll do our best, both of us.
lunardi.r2: Thank you, Ettore. We'll do our best, both of us.

esito.ok: The doctor saw Nina in time, and she got out of bed before evening, books under her arm.
esito.fallita: Nina still has the fever. The doctor passed under her window twice, without being able to go up.

gino.testo: don piero is cofing and cant say mass so who rings the bell?? cure him before one. and when im better i want to see the litehouse lantern from INSIDE. promise??
gino.r1: Get better first. The lantern can wait, and so can Zeno.
gino.r2: From inside, I promise. But the priest first: he knows how to ring the bell.

esito.ok: The priest is cured. Gino has already tried the bell rope, just to be sure.
esito.fallita: The priest is still coughing, and on Sunday the bell will stay silent. Gino took it badly.

nina.testo: Dad has the fever and says it's nothing, like he said about Mum. Cure him, please. I'll hold out: I held out against Leopardi, I can hold out against anything.

esito.ok: Bepi is cured, and said it was nothing. Nina cried in the kitchen, where he couldn't see her.
esito.fallita: Bepi is still burning. Nina changed his cold cloths all night, as her mother used to.

hint.spinta: Zeno never strays more than two places from the Lighthouse: the priest must go to him.
hint.indizio: Teresa reads any letter she holds at an hour's end: she must pass it on in the first row.

prete.1: Father, I must give something back. And ask forgiveness of someone who isn't here.
prete.2: Then this evening, Zeno. Before dark. At night some things weigh more.

sera.1: She gave it to me, at two. She passed over me like a wave.
sera.2: I never could say no to that family.

ammessa.1: Accepted! Teacher-training in Venice, with a boarding place from Easter. It's stamped!
ammessa.2: Now comes the hard part: telling Dad before the Pier finds out.

letta.1: Accepted, dear! I read it first, I couldn't resist. Such a lovely envelope.
letta.2: The whole island knows before my father. Thank you, Teresa. Really.
letta.1d: Accepted, miss! I read it first, I couldn't resist.

lanterna.1: I saw the lantern! Not lit, though. Zeno won't light it in the daytime!
lanterna.2: By day the Lighthouse sleeps. Come back one evening, when the light has work to do.

zeno.testo: Tomorrow I must speak to the priest. I have something that isn't mine, and someone to ask forgiveness of. Get me to him. On my own I won't come down to the village.
zeno.r2: You'll get there. I'll bring the priest to you, in my arms if need be.

esito.ok: Zeno came down to the village and talked to the priest, a long while, under the porch. Neither would say what about.
esito.fallita: Zeno didn't make it to the priest. Tonight, he says, he'll come down anyway: some things won't wait any longer.

teresa.testo: Dear, a silly question: if one day a letter came for me, just one, would you bring it to me? For thirty years I've carried everyone else's.
teresa.r1: If it comes, I'll bring it. Without opening it.
teresa.r2: Who would write to you? Tell me.

nina.testo: The result from the teacher-training college has come. The postwoman has it, and the postwoman reads everything, even the stamps. Let it reach me by noon. Sealed.

esito.ok: The result reached Nina sealed, the stamp unbroken. She opened it alone, on the Pier, and shouted.
esito.fallita: The exam envelope didn't arrive as it should, sealed and in time. Nina said thank you anyway, through her teeth.

gino.testo: zeno is taking me to the litehouse at one!!! to see the lantern. dont tell mum. and not teresa eether or mum will know

esito.ok: Gino climbed the Lighthouse at one. He came down with hands black with grease and eyes full of glass.
esito.fallita: At one Gino was far from the Lighthouse. Zeno waited for him at the top of the stairs, with the door open.

hint.spinta: Bepi returns at eight in the evening, come what may. Whoever's at the Pier then meets him.
hint.indizio: Zeno never strays from the Lighthouse: keep him in the last column from six to eight.

luce.1: The light was there. I followed it to the Pier with my eyes shut, like when I was a boy.
luce.2: Dad, you're soaked through. You're in one piece. Never go out in a storm again.

secca.1: The Lighthouse was dark. I hit the shoal bow first, and the oar caught my arm.
secca.2: The arm will heal, Mr Scarpa. For a month, no oars and no wine.

nero.1: At the top edge of the lace, far off, the black thread is back. Closer than last time.
nero.2: Someone out there is weaving. I feel it the way you feel the wind before the wave.

campane.1: I rang till I couldn't feel my arms. From seven to eight, without stopping.
campane.2: The Lord and the fishermen heard. Let us hope in the right order.

molo.1: At seven Gino wasn't home: he ran off to watch the waves in the storm.
molo.2: A fisherman brought him back, soaked. I dried him by the oven, without a word.

nina.testo: Dad went out fishing and the sea has turned. Let Zeno stay at the Lighthouse with the light on from six to eight in the evening, the whole time. And at seven take me to the Pier, to wait for him. Please. Please.

esito.ok: The Lighthouse light stayed lit until eight, and Nina was at the Pier waiting. Bepi came home whole, and Nina slept.
esito.fallita: Something was missing, the Lighthouse light or Nina at the Pier, and Bepi's boat hit the shallows. Tonight Nina hasn't written me a word.
esito.lasciato: I let Nina's request drop. Nobody kept the Lighthouse light for Bepi.

marta.testo: In this wind Gino doesn't go out. At seven in the evening I want him home, at the bakery, with me: the water takes boys, and I haven't another son.

esito.ok: At seven Gino was home, at the bakery. Marta baked bread twice, to keep her hands busy.
esito.fallita: At seven Gino wasn't home: he was out, with the storm on top of him. Marta hasn't spoken to anyone tonight, not even to the oven.

piero.testo: At seven in the evening I'll ring the storm bells, as they did in the old days. Let me be in church: the boats at sea must hear them, and know that here we pray.

esito.ok: At seven in the evening the storm bells rang. From the sea, someone answered with a whistle.
esito.fallita: At seven the priest wasn't in church, and the bells stayed silent. The wind rang on its own.

gino.testo: I WANT TO SEE THE STORM FROM THE LITEHOUSE WITH ZENO!!! at 7 in the evening. im not scared. a bit yes but not much
gino.r1: Tonight the Lighthouse is Zeno's and the light's.
gino.r2: Watch it from the window, with your mum beside you.

esito.ok: Gino watched the storm from the Lighthouse, beside Zeno. He says the waves were as tall as the church.
esito.fallita: Gino didn't get to the Lighthouse. He watched the heavy sea from the window, his nose on the glass.

sera.vuota: Tonight the lagoon brings nothing: it is black, and the wind is rising.

perline.fascio: the bundle of L.'s letters for Ada, to go to Zeno
perline.confessione: Teresa's confession, shut in the well
perline.segretoNina: Nina's secret about her packed suitcase

hint.spinta: With three secrets the well overflows: at its next crossing from on top, it gives it all.
hint.indizio: Nina on top of Marta takes both secrets to the well; then the bundle goes to Zeno.

trabocco.1: I thought I was keeping sins. They were letters.

fascio.1: They're yours, little one. A hundred and sixty-eight. One a month, for fourteen years.
fascio.1d: They're yours, miss. A hundred and sixty-eight. One a month, for fourteen years.
fascio.2: Read them slowly. I'll wait outside, with the sea.
fascio.2d: Read them slowly, miss. I'll wait outside with the sea.

sepolte.1: A bundle of letters? Under the altar cloths. I don't know whose they are.
sepolte.2: L.'s letters stay in the well. Out there, someone is still waiting for them.

teresa.1: It fell into my hands, dear. I held it an hour and didn't open it, I swear.
teresa.2: All right, I read one. Just one. They were for you.
teresa.2d: All right, I read one. Just one. They were for the lacemaker.
teresa.1d: It fell into my hands, miss. I held it an hour and didn't open it.

marta.1: My secret is still mine. It weighs the same, but it's mine.
marta.2: The priest looked at me the way you look at a cold oven. So be it.

zeno.testo: The priest keeps a bundle of letters he doesn't know he has. They're yours, but you have no thread: get them to me by five, and I'll bring them. I waited for them too.

esito.ok: The bundle came out of the well and reached Zeno before five. My mother's letters, after fourteen years, are on their way.
esito.fallita: The bundle never left the well, or didn't reach Zeno by five. Zeno waited at his door until dark.
esito.lasciato: I let the bundle drop. My mother's letters stay in the well, ten steps from home.

teresa.testo: Dear, I've decided: I'll read nothing more that isn't mine. But I can't do it alone, letters fall into my hands like cherries. Tomorrow at two take me to the Bakery, far from that bundle.
teresa.r1: You'll manage. I'll watch you from the lace pillow.
teresa.r2: Those letters are my mother's. Let them arrive whole.

esito.ok: At two Teresa was at the Bakery, and she never touched the bundle. She walked past the church with her hands in her pockets, on purpose.
esito.fallita: Teresa didn't keep away from the bundle as she wished: at two she wasn't at the Bakery, or it passed through her bag.

piero.testo: Free me, my child. I hold more secrets in my breast than one man can keep, and I no longer know which are mine. Send me by one whoever has something to confess. Domine, non sum dignus.
piero.r1: I'll free you. But first tell me what you're keeping, and for whom.
piero.r2: What you keep isn't all yours. Giving it back is half the forgiveness.

esito.ok: By one, Nina's and Marta's secrets had reached the priest. The well was full; now, he says, it can breathe.
esito.fallita: By one, the secrets he asked for hadn't reached the priest. He prayed alone, his hands on the altar cloths.

marta.testo: What I have to tell the priest I tell the Lord, with no go-between. My secret stays mine, like my sourdough starter. Tomorrow at two I'm at my Bakery, and no confession.

esito.ok: At two Marta was at her Bakery, and her secret never reached the priest. The bread came out better.
esito.fallita: At two Marta wasn't at her Bakery, or her secret ended up in the well. She hasn't forgiven me, but she brought me bread all the same.

margine.trabocco: Even wells fill up: with three secrets Don Piero overflows, and gives all from above.
margine.traboccato: The well has given everything back: what it kept is on its way again.

perline.medicina: the doctor's only dose for the school

eco.1: The school first. Six children, and in my bag I have a single dose.
eco.2: Marta stepped aside without a word. They hadn't spoken for twenty-two years already.
eco.3: Teresa, I've nothing left in my bag. Tomorrow I'll come back with more medicine.
eco.4: Miss Teresa, why are you running? Where are you off to in such a hurry?
eco.5: I'm going to Venice for more medicine. I'll be back tomorrow, on the first ferry.

rivela.1: In 1958 Grandmother sent the doctor to the school. Nobody came to Aldo.
rivela.2: Aldo wanted to take Teresa to the mainland the next summer. There was no next summer.

arc3.margine: One for six. And one who stayed.

guida.nomina: Who carries the medicine, who has the fever? Threads are known by what they do.
guida.strappo: Nine and ten are torn: weave them again as they were, up to the eleven o'clock row.

hint.spinta: The thread with the medicine is the doctor. The one with the fever, nobody reaches.
hint.indizio: The mending is right when at eleven every thread is where the recorded row finds it.

perline.L_ada: a letter from Livia for Ada, who is two

eco.1: Here's the suitcase, Livia. Have a good trip, and come back soon.
eco.2: Don Piero, you keep it. Give it to her when she's old enough.
eco.3: Where are you going, Livia, with that suitcase? At this hour, with the baby at home?
eco.4: The nine o'clock ferry, madam. On you get, we're leaving. The sea is calm.
eco.5: A trip, she'd said. A trip. And I'm the one who carried her suitcase.

rivela.1: In 1951 Grandmother wove my mother to the Pier, at ferry time.
rivela.2: Zeno carried her suitcase. Her letter for me ended up in Don Piero's well.

guida.nomina: A suitcase, a letter for a two-year-old girl: who carries them, and to whom?
guida.strappo: Seven and eight are torn: weave them again, and at nine whoever is at the Pier leaves.

hint.spinta: The suitcase-bearer never strays from the Lighthouse. Its owner is at the Pier by nine.
hint.indizio: The little girl's letter ends up with the one who takes everything and never gives.

desiderio.teresa: Teresa wants a letter written for her. In thirty years she has carried thousands, and read too many. None was hers, and she knows it by heart.
desiderio.marta: Marta wants Gino not to leave the way Ernesto did. She says it kneading, without looking up, the way you say something that has hurt for thirty years.
desiderio.piero: Don Piero wants to give back what he keeps. All of it: letters, secrets, years. He says a full well quenches no one's thirst.
desiderio.bepi: Bepi wants to say goodbye to Nina properly, before she goes. He doesn't know how, and won't ask anyone, but he wants it more than his boat.
desiderio.zeno: Zeno wants to ask forgiveness of someone who is no longer here. He won't say whom, or for what: he looks at the sea towards Chioggia and keeps quiet.
desiderio.lunardi: Dr Lunardi wants the island to call him by his name. Ettore. So far here they call him “the stranger”, or “the doctor”, or nothing.

lunardi.arrivo: Dr Lunardi comes from Padua. He says “excuse me” and “thank you”, and wears his hat even in the wind. Nobody here trusts a man so polite.
lunardi.cura: Lunardi never falls ill. If he's on top of a sick person, he cures them: the cure beats the contagion. If he's below, he cures no one.
lunardi.passo: Lunardi walks slowly, as in the city. To cure someone he must pass over them; if he only passes by, the fever stays where it is.
lunardi.nome: A name passes like a rumour. Whoever gets it remembers me; whoever doesn't, little by little, forgets.
lunardi.ettore: I called him Ettore, and the doctor went red to the ears. In Padua, he says, nobody called him that.
lunardi.scarpa: Lunardi cured Bepi with a hand on his forehead. Bepi will never thank him out loud, but now he greets him with a nod of the chin.
lunardi.nomeNo: Lunardi asked everyone my name, and nobody could answer. Here, a name is passed from hand to hand.
lunardi.dottore: I thanked the doctor and called him “Doctor”, like everyone does. He smiled anyway, but only with his mouth.

teresa.borsa: Teresa carries the whole island's post in her bag. If anyone brushes against it, half the Fondamenta knows by evening.
teresa.lettera: Teresa has carried other people's letters for thirty years. One for her has never come, and every morning she looks at the sack like someone waiting.
teresa.trentanni: Teresa counts the years since that day in '36: thirty. Marta doesn't count them, but she knows them by heart too.
teresa.esame: Teresa read Nina's result before she did. The whole island knew it, before her father.
teresa.fascio: Teresa held my mother's bundle and read one. Just one, she says. She asked my forgiveness twice.
teresa.dottoreFiducia: I wrote to Teresa that the doctor cures people and doesn't read the post. She says whoever doesn't read the post knows nothing about anyone.
teresa.dottoreSospetto: I promised Teresa to keep the doctor at the other end of the Fondamenta. A lace-pillow promise: it costs thread, and she doesn't know it.
teresa.promessa: I promised Teresa to keep an eye on her from the lace pillow, and she promised to stop reading. We'll see which of us keeps her word.
teresa.sa: I told Teresa those letters are my mother's. She was silent for a whole minute. For Teresa, that's an eternity.

bepi.dottore: Bepi won't open the door to the mainland doctor. He treats himself with wine, with silence, and with Nina bringing him broth.
bepi.debito: Bepi has a debt in Chioggia, for the good net. If Nina knows, she heard it from the street and not from him.
bepi.luce: In the storm Bepi followed the Lighthouse beam all the way home. Zeno didn't sleep a wink, and neither did Nina.
bepi.secca: In the storm Bepi ran aground, with the Lighthouse dark. His arm will heal; the boat, perhaps. Nina hasn't spoken to him for two days, out of fear.
bepi.febbre: On the longest night the doctor never got as far as the Pier. Bepi still has the fever, and Nina isn't studying.
bepi.apre: I told Bepi to let the doctor see him, for Nina if not for himself. He left the door ajar. For Bepi, that's a yes.
bepi.tacere: I promised Bepi that Nina won't hear of the debt from me. But the island is small, and Teresa's bag is big.

marta.nodo: If Teresa and Marta cross, they knot: they stand still an hour and pass nothing, not even a greeting. The knot stays drawn in the lace.
marta.forno: In the week of the fever Marta's bakery stayed open, except for one hour: Gino's. Nobody dared complain.
marta.segreto: Marta still keeps Ernesto's letter, the one from '36. She never told the priest, and perhaps not even the Lord.
marta.confessione: Marta didn't confess. Her secret is still hers: it weighs the same, she says, but it's hers.
marta.fornoChiuso: I told Marta to shut the bakery for an hour and stay with Gino. For the first time in thirty years, the bread waited.
marta.promessa: I promised Marta that Gino will get well and stay with her. I still don't know why someone leaving frightens her so.
marta.perche: I asked Marta what Teresa did to her. She didn't answer: she kneaded harder, as if the dough knew.
marta.largo: Marta has steered clear of Teresa for thirty years. I told her to carry on, if it does her good. I don't know if it does.

gino.pagella: The teacher wrote WELL DONE on Gino's report. In Italian. In arithmetic, less so: there it says “must try harder”, which is another way of putting it.
gino.febbre: Gino with a fever stays in bed: for once he doesn't run. Anyone who crosses him, though, catches it.
gino.tempesta: In the storm Gino ran off to watch the waves instead of staying home. Marta dried him in silence, which is worse than a scolding.
gino.guarito: Gino got well on the longest night. He ate two loaves and was running again before breakfast.
gino.faro: Gino saw the lantern by day, unlit. Zeno told him to come back one evening, when the light is working.
gino.casa: I told Gino that tonight the Lighthouse belongs to Zeno and the light. He answered with a drawing of a lighthouse, angry, with eyes.
gino.finestra: Gino will watch the storm from the window, with his mum beside him. He says it's the same. It isn't, but that's all right.

nina.ammessa: Nina has a place at the teacher-training college in Venice, boarding from Easter. She's already decided where she'll sit: front row, by the window.
nina.venezia: Nina keeps the Venice ferry timetable under her pillow. She knows it by heart, like Leopardi, and recites it to fall asleep.
nina.valigia: Nina has a suitcase packed under her bed. It's the worst-kept secret on the island: even the well knows.
nina.febbre: Nina caught the fever from Gino, hand to hand. She reads Manzoni in bed, and says it's the right moment.
nina.debito: Nina has found out about the debt. Bepi won't speak to anyone any more.

zeno.lettera: Zeno kept Grandmother's letter for me all this time. She gave it to him herself, at two, passing over him like a wave.
zeno.calligrafia: Zeno spends his afternoons looking at the sea towards Chioggia. He says you don't forget handwriting, not even after fourteen years.

piero.trabocca: Even wells fill up. With three secrets Don Piero overflows, and at his first crossing from on top he gives away all he keeps, letters included.
piero.messa: Don Piero said mass for the healthy without falling ill. He says the credit is the Lord's; I know some of it is the lace pillow's.
piero.campane: In the storm Don Piero rang the bells as in the old days. The boats at sea heard them, and prayed with him.
piero.febbre: Don Piero caught the fever and said mass all the same. He says the Lord forgives. Fever doesn't.
piero.curato: Don Piero is well again, and on Sunday Gino will ring the bell. Out of tune, the priest said, like everything here.

livia.lettere: I've read three of my mother's letters. The other hundred and sixty-five I read slowly, one each evening, like a rosary.

ada.nome: Every night I pin my name on a thread. Whoever doesn't get it calls me “miss” the next day, and then nothing at all.
ada.g09: With the doctor came the fever, or perhaps the other way round. The island looks at Lunardi the way you look at the sea in winter: from far off.
ada.g10: In the week of the fever I understood something: whoever cures must be on top, and whoever loves wants to be near. It isn't always the same thing.
ada.g11: Teresa and Marta knotted on my lace pillow, or steered clear of each other. Either way, the knot is there.
ada.g12: From tonight I pin my name to a thread. If I don't, the island forgets me a little at a time, the way you forget a song.
ada.g13: The longest night: four sick, one doctor, the thread counted. I tried not to choose, and the thread told me what it costs.
ada.g14: My mother is alive. Her name is Livia. I read Grandmother's letter three times, then put it under my pillow.
ada.g15: During the storm the black thread came back to the edge of the lace. Someone outside is weaving towards us.
ada.g16: Now I know where my mother's letters were: ten steps from home, under the altar cloths, for fourteen years.
ada.arc3: I mended the 1958 lace. Grandmother knew perfectly well who she was leaving behind: she wrote it in the margin, in her neatest hand.
ada.arc4: I saw my mother board the nine o'clock ferry, in 1951. I was two and asleep. Grandmother, in the margin: “Not yet.”

puntoAperto.pagina: A page torn from the Book of Stitches: the drawing of a nameless stitch, where no thread is held. Grandmother never explained it.

anno1958.cassapanca: In the chest there is a lace dated 1958. If I say that year, Teresa crosses the street and Marta crosses herself.
anno1958.notte: Four sick, a single doctor, and the thread counted. In the chest, the 1958 lace has the same shape as last night.
anno1958.risposta: In 1958 Grandmother saved the six schoolchildren and left the fever to Aldo, Teresa's fiancé.
anno1958.pista: Where to look: with the fever, the island's old folk say “like in fifty-eight” and change the subject. Teresa speaks of a certain Aldo only when it rains.

chiL.risposta: L. is Livia, my mother. She is alive, in Chioggia. She has written to me since I was two, and her letters never arrived.

avorio.lettera: The ivory thread was Grandmother: the last time she wove herself in, to give Zeno the letter for me.

madre.apre: Grandmother sent my mother away on the nine o'clock ferry. Why? In the chest there's a lace from 1951 I haven't opened yet.
madre.risposta: My mother wanted an open lace, where people choose for themselves. Grandmother, afraid, wove her to the Pier at ferry time.
madre.pista: Where to look: the 1951 lace is still waiting in the chest. If I say that year, Zeno looks at the sea towards Chioggia.

pozzo.pista: Don Piero keeps something he doesn't know he has. Where to look: a well overflows when it holds three secrets.
pozzo.risposta: Don Piero was keeping my mother's letters: a hundred and sixty-eight, one a month for fourteen years. He didn't know he had them.
pozzo.sepolte: My mother's letters are still in the well. Where to look: to free them, it must overflow, with three secrets.

filoNero.pista: Where to look: during the storm the black thread came back to the top edge of the lace. In one of the first bottles, L. spoke of sepia black.

arc3.aldo: Aldo was Teresa's fiancé. The next summer he would have taken her to the mainland, and Grandmother wanted no one to leave.
arc3.scuola: Dr Bortolo had a single dose. Grandmother sent him to the school, to the six children. Nobody came to Aldo.

arc4.valigia: Zeno carried my mother's suitcase thinking it was a trip. He hasn't forgiven himself since, and watches the sea towards Chioggia.
arc4.lettera: Before boarding the ferry, my mother gave Don Piero a letter for me. It ended up in the well, the first of them all.

lettere.bottiglia_nodo_nero: After the storm the lagoon brought an empty bottle. Inside, a knot of black thread. Nobody writes any more: someone weaves.
lettere.fascio: The bundle of my mother's letters: three readable and a hundred and sixty-five more, tied with bakery string. One a month, for fourteen years.
lettere.clotilde: Grandmother's letter is in the sepia hand of the Book's margins. At the bottom, a single letter: C. As on the note pinned to the lace pillow.

lettere.lettera_L8: My dear, this year you turn sixteen. At sixteen I wanted to leave and to stay, both at once. I hope you manage one of the two. L.
lettere.lettera_L9: My dear, in Chioggia the women clean fish on their doorsteps and sing. I don't sing, but I clean fish beautifully by now: my hands are full of little cuts that don't hurt any more. Sometimes I think hands know how to do things the head never decided. Yours, who knows. I hope they can't clean fish. L.
lettere.lettera_L10: My dear, today I saw a little girl with plaits waiting for the ferry alone, serious as a notary, with a bag bigger than she was. It wasn't you, I know: you're grown now, and perhaps you don't wear plaits any more. But for a moment I stopped breathing, and the ferry left without me. I took the next one. L.
lettere.lettera_L11: My dear, she's dead, isn't she? Last night the sea was different. I'm coming. I don't know how yet. L.
lettere.lettera_clotilde:
Ada,
if Zeno gives you this letter, it means the ivory thread held until three, and that I am gone.
Your mother is alive. Her name is Livia, and it was I who sent her away, on the nine o'clock ferry, when you were two. She wanted to weave an open lace, to let people choose for themselves. I was afraid. I had seen what people do when they choose for themselves.
She has written to you every month. The letters are with Don Piero: I made sure they went there, one by one, for fourteen years. He doesn't even know he is keeping them.
I did other things too. You will find them in the chest. I don't ask you to forgive me.
I ask one thing only: don't believe anyone who tells you the island needs a lacemaker. I believed it for sixty years.
Two lacemakers on the same lace tear it. That much, at least, is true. I think.
C.
lettere.fascio_1: My Ada, today you are two and a half and I am in Chioggia, in a room that smells of nets. I left you with your grandmother because it was the only way to leave you a whole island, with the bakery, the church and the Lighthouse. One day you'll understand, or you won't, and that will be all right too. I'll write every month, I promise. Don Piero will bring you the letters; he's a good man. Mum
lettere.fascio_2: My Ada, you are nine. They say there's fever on the island, and that the schoolchildren have all got well, one after another. I cried in the middle of the market like a fool, with the fish crates all around me. I know who deserves the credit, and I know what it cost. Someone always pays for that kind of credit. Keep your neck covered, and don't run about when you're sweaty. Mum
lettere.fascio_3: My Ada, fifteen. I no longer know what your face looks like: I picture you with your grandmother's nose, though I hope not. I've learned to weave on my own, in sepia black, which doesn't show on blue velvet. I'm not using it yet. I keep it ready, the way you keep a suitcase under the bed. The day she is gone, I'm coming. Mum
